examples: The room is dark. I turn on the light.
Please turn off the light when you leave.
nuance: 전등 is an electric light or lamp, usually the main light in a room or on the ceiling. In everyday speech many Koreans just say 불 (as in 불 켜다 / 불 끄다) for turning lights on and off. Use 켜다 to turn it on and 끄다 to turn it off.
mistakes: Turn a light on/off with 켜다/끄다, not 열다/닫다 (those are for doors).
In casual speech 불 켜다 / 불 끄다 is more common than 전등을 켜다.

examples: 나가다 here = burn out / stop working
I changed it for a new bulb.
I need to buy one light bulb.
nuance: 전구 is the light bulb itself — the small part you screw into a lamp or fixture. When a bulb burns out, Koreans say 전구가 나갔어요 (the bulb went out). Use 갈다 (replace) when you put in a new one. Count bulbs with 개.
mistakes: Do not confuse 전구 (the bulb) with 전등 (the whole lamp/light).
When a bulb stops working say 나갔어요 or 나갔다; 죽었어요 is unnatural for a bulb.

usage: I turn on the desk lamp
I turn off the desk lamp
examples: I turn on the desk lamp when I read.
I turn off the lamp before sleeping.
nuance: 스탠드 (from English 'stand') is a small desk or table lamp, the kind you use for reading or studying. It is the everyday word for a desk lamp in Korean. The fuller form 스탠드 조명 or 전기스탠드 also exists, but plain 스탠드 is most common.
mistakes: Here 스탠드 means a desk lamp, not a place to 'stand' or a stadium stand.
Turn it on/off with 켜다/끄다, the same verbs used for any light.

usage: There is a calendar on the wall
I mark it on the calendar
examples: There is a calendar hanging on the wall.
I check the date on the calendar.
It's the new year, so I changed the calendar.
nuance: 달력 is a physical calendar — the wall or desk kind with the months and dates printed on it. It literally combines 달 (month) + 력 (calendar). For a schedule or planner you keep appointments in, Koreans use 일정 or 다이어리; 달력 is the date grid itself.
mistakes: Do not confuse 달력 (calendar) with 달 (the moon / a month) — though they share the 달 syllable.
A personal schedule/planner is 일정 or 다이어리, not 달력.

examples: I put the family photo in a frame.
I hung a frame on the wall.
nuance: 액자 is a frame that holds a photo or a picture, the kind you stand on a shelf or hang on the wall. You put a 사진 (photo) or 그림 (picture) inside it. Use 걸다 (hang) for putting it on a wall and 넣다 (put in) for placing a photo inside.
mistakes: 액자 is the frame; the photo inside is 사진 — do not mix the two words.
Hang a frame with 걸다, not 붙이다 (붙이다 is for sticking flat things on).

examples: There is a potted plant by the window.
I water the plant every day.
My friend gave me a potted plant.
nuance: 화분 is a flowerpot or potted plant — the pot together with the plant growing in it. To water it, say 화분에 물을 줘요 (literally 'give water to the pot'). The flower itself is 꽃 and a plant is 식물, while 화분 is specifically the potted container.
mistakes: 화분 is the pot/potted plant; a single flower is 꽃 — do not confuse them.
Water a plant with 물을 주다, not 물을 마시다 (which is for a person drinking).

examples: There are a lot of cushions on the sofa.
I watch TV hugging a cushion.
nuance: 쿠션 (from English 'cushion') is a soft throw cushion or pillow you put on a sofa, bed, or chair to lean on or hug. It is different from 베개, which is specifically the pillow you sleep on. 쿠션 pairs naturally with 푹신하다 (soft and fluffy).
mistakes: Do not confuse 쿠션 (a soft cushion for sitting/leaning) with 베개 (a pillow for sleeping).
A floor sitting cushion in Korean homes is 방석, slightly different from a 쿠션.

usage: I cover myself with a blanket
examples: It was cold, so I covered up with a blanket.
I put a blanket over my knees.
I folded the blanket and put it on the sofa.
nuance: 담요 is a light blanket or throw, the kind you put over your lap or shoulders when you are cold. It is thinner than 이불, the thick quilt/duvet you sleep under. Use 덮다 (cover) to put it over yourself and 개다 (fold) for folding bedding.
mistakes: Do not confuse 담요 (light blanket/throw) with 이불 (thick sleeping quilt/duvet).
Fold bedding with 개다, not 접다 (접다 is for folding paper).

usage: I throw it in the trash can
examples: Please throw the trash in the trash can.
nuance: 쓰레기통 combines 쓰레기 (trash) + 통 (bin/container), meaning the trash can or wastebasket. You throw garbage into it with 버리다. Note that in Korea trash is sorted, so you may also hear 분리수거함 for the recycling bins specifically.
mistakes: Throw trash away with 버리다, not 던지다 (which means to throw/toss forcefully).
쓰레기통 is one word; do not add a space inside it.

examples: I sweep the floor with a broom.
I swept the yard with a broom.
nuance: 빗자루 is a broom for sweeping the floor, used together with the verb 쓸다 (to sweep). It often pairs with a 쓰레받기 (dustpan). Use the particle 로/으로 to say you sweep 'with' a broom: 빗자루로 쓸어요.
mistakes: Sweep with 쓸다, not 닦다 (닦다 is for wiping a surface with a cloth).
Do not confuse 빗자루 (broom) with 빗 (a hair comb), even though they look similar.

examples: I wipe the floor with a rag.
The rag was dirty, so I washed it.
I spilled water, so I wiped it with a rag.
nuance: 걸레 is a cleaning rag or floor cloth used for wiping floors and surfaces, paired with 닦다 (wipe). The act of mopping the floor with it is 걸레질. Wash a dirty rag with 빨다 (the verb for washing cloth/laundry), not the dish-washing verb.
mistakes: Do not confuse 걸레 (a dirty-work cleaning rag) with 행주 (a clean kitchen dishcloth) or 수건 (a towel).
Wash a cloth with 빨다, not 씻다 (씻다 is for washing your body or dishes).

examples: I iron the shirt with the iron.
The iron is hot, so be careful.
I turn on the iron and wait.
nuance: 다리미 is a clothes iron, the appliance, used with the verb 다리다 (to iron). Be careful not to mix up the noun 다리미 (iron) with the verb 다리다 (to iron) — they look similar. The ironing board is a separate item, 다리미판.
mistakes: 다리미 is the iron (the tool); the action 'to iron' is the verb 다리다.
Do not confuse 다리미 (iron) with 다리 (leg / bridge) — different words.

usage: There is a clock on the wall
I look at the wall clock
examples: There is a wall clock hanging on the wall.
I check the time on the wall clock.
The clock stopped. I need to change the battery.
nuance: 벽시계 combines 벽 (wall) + 시계 (clock), meaning a wall clock. It is hung on the wall with 걸다 and you read the time from it. A wristwatch is 손목시계 and an alarm clock is 알람시계 — all built on the base word 시계.
mistakes: 벽시계 is one word for a wall clock; 손목시계 (wristwatch) is a different compound.
Hang a clock with 걸다; it 'is hanging' as 걸려 있어요.

examples: I laid a mat on the floor.
The baby plays on the mat.
nuance: 매트 (from English 'mat') is a flat mat you lay on the floor — for exercise (요가 매트), for a baby to play on, or by the door (현관 매트). You spread it out with 깔다 (lay/spread). A thicker sleeping mattress is 매트리스, a related but different word.
mistakes: Lay a mat down with 깔다, not 놓다 (놓다 is for placing an object on a surface).
Do not confuse 매트 (a flat mat) with 매트리스 (a thick bed mattress).
